summary: This document gives functional requirements for supporting the Metro Ethernet Forum E-Tree service in multipoint Layer 2 VPN solutions. Future solutions are meant to use these requirements as guidelines.

plainLanguage.summary: An E-Tree service has one or more root sites and many leaf sites. Leaves may talk to the roots, and roots may talk to everyone, but leaves may not talk to each other. This RFC lists what a carrier's layer 2 VPN has to do to offer that, because today's VPLS gives every site a path to every other site.

subtitle: What an L2VPN solution has to do to offer a rooted multipoint Ethernet service with leaf-to-leaf traffic blocked.

tldr.problem: Providers offer Ethernet LAN services to customers using VPLS, but they also need to offer a rooted multipoint service, E-Tree, where a leaf site can talk to the root but not to the other leaves.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains why VPLS cannot do this: it treats every attachment circuit alike and gives any-to-any connectivity, so a receiving router cannot tell which circuit a frame arrived on. It then states three functional requirements, plus requirements on applicability, backward compatibility and the external network interface.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC written as guidance for future solutions rather than a protocol. It also answers the common question of whether the Virtual Private Multicast Service requirements already cover this, and concludes they do not.

facts.label: Traffic flows in a generic E-Tree

today: RFC 7152 is an Informational RFC published in March 2014. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains a statement of requirements for future E-Tree solutions rather than a protocol of its own.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The document provides functional requirements for supporting the Metro Ethernet Forum Ethernet Tree service, E-Tree, in multipoint Layer 2 Virtual Private Network solutions, which it calls simply L2VPN. It is intended that potential solutions use these requirements as guidelines.

A considerable number of service providers have adopted Virtual Private LAN Service to provide MEF Ethernet LAN services to customers. Those providers currently need a simple and effective way to emulate E-Tree services in addition to E-LAN services on their MPLS networks, and they also expect E-Tree support in any newly developed L2VPN technology.
sections.plainLanguage: Carriers already sell a flat Ethernet service over their MPLS networks. This RFC says what they would need to add to sell a tree-shaped one, where the branches cannot talk to each other.

sections.title: The IETF L2VPN Services
sections.content:
VPLS, described in RFC 4761 and RFC 4762, is an L2VPN service that provides multipoint-to-multipoint connectivity for Ethernet across an IP or MPLS-enabled packet switched network. It emulates the VLAN functionality of traditional Ethernet networks. The customer Ethernet frame is transported over the packet switched network from the ingress provider edge to the egress provider edge, where the destination is chosen from the frame's destination MAC address in the context of the virtual switching instance to which it belongs.

E-VPN is an enhanced layer 2 service that emulates an Ethernet VLAN across an IP/MPLS packet switched network, primarily targeted at large-scale L2VPNs with resiliency requirements that other solutions do not meet. The RFC notes that E-VPN was under development at the time of writing and refers readers to its own requirements document.
sections.plainLanguage: Two IETF technologies are in scope: VPLS, which many carriers already run, and E-VPN, which was being written at the time.

sections.title: E-LAN and E-Tree
sections.content:
MEF has defined two multipoint Ethernet service types: E-LAN, a multipoint-to-multipoint service, and E-Tree, a rooted-multipoint service.

They are similar in that the data frame is an Ethernet frame, the data forwarding is MAC-based, and a generic service of either kind is bidirectional in the sense that ingress frames can originate at any endpoint. The difference is in how endpoints are classified. Within a multipoint Ethernet service each endpoint is designated either a Root or a Leaf. A Root can communicate with all other endpoints in the same service, while a Leaf can only communicate with Roots. E-LAN has Root endpoints only, which means there is no communication restriction between endpoints. E-Tree has both Root and Leaf endpoints, which means a restriction between Leaf endpoints has to be enforced.

The RFC lists the use cases that drive this. A hub and spoke VPN puts the hub site at the Root and the spoke sites at the Leaves. Wholesale access puts the customer's interconnect at the Root and the customer's subscribers at the Leaves. Mobile backhaul puts the radio access network controller at the Root and the base stations at the Leaves. Precision clock synchronisation puts the PTP server at the Root and the clients at the Leaves. Internet access puts the broadband network gateway at the Root and the subscriber at the Leaf. Broadcast video puts the video source at the Root and the subscribers at the Leaves, and the broadcast and multicast variant adds a control channel. Device management puts the management system at the Root and the managed devices at the Leaves. Common to all of them, direct layer 2 leaf-to-leaf communication is not required or must be inhibited, and where leaf-to-leaf traffic is disallowed for security reasons, E-Tree is the way to prohibit it.

A generic E-Tree service supports multiple Root endpoints, usually for redundancy, though whether a particular service needs one or several depends on the application. It supports five flows: unicast from Root to Leaf, unicast from Leaf to Root, unicast from Root to Root, broadcast or multicast from Root to the other Roots and Leaves, and broadcast or multicast from Leaf to the Roots. A particular service may need only a subset.

The appendix answers a common question about whether the Virtual Private Multicast Service requirements already cover this. They do not. VPMS focuses on point-to-multipoint connectivity, provides single coverage of receiver membership with no distinct differentiation between multiple multicast groups, and does not use the destination address in an Ethernet frame for data forwarding. It may support reverse traffic from a Leaf to a Root as an optional capability. In contrast, the focus of MEF E-Tree is that a Leaf can only communicate with Roots and not with Leaves, and a generic E-Tree service supports multiple Root endpoints. The two definitions are significantly different. VPMS may be acceptable where no unicast traffic from the Root is destined for a specific Leaf, and where there is no traffic between Roots. For a generic E-Tree service, VPMS will not meet the requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Both services carry Ethernet frames and forward by MAC address. The difference is that an E-LAN has only roots, so nothing is blocked, while an E-Tree has leaves, and leaves are cut off from each other.

sections.title: Why VPLS Cannot Do It
sections.content:
The RFC uses VPLS to illustrate the problem, and notes that the same principle applies to other L2VPN technologies. VPLS treats all attachment circuits equally, essentially as Roots, although they are not classified as Root or Leaf, and provides any-to-any connectivity among them. VPLS has no mechanism for restricting communication between specific attachment circuits, so it is insufficient for emulating a generic E-Tree service.

The worked example has two provider edges, each with a Root attachment circuit and a Leaf attachment circuit, connected by an Ethernet pseudowire. When the second provider edge receives a frame from the first over that pseudowire, three things are true at once: it does not know which attachment circuit on the first edge the frame came in on, it does not know whether that circuit was a Leaf, and it does not have enough information to enforce the leaf-to-leaf restriction. The cases that break are a Leaf sending a broadcast or multicast frame, and a Leaf sending a unicast frame addressed to the MAC address of another Leaf on the far side.

The RFC notes that there are ways around this problem that do not require extensions to existing VPLS solutions, but they all carry significant design complexity or deployment constraints.
sections.plainLanguage: When a frame arrives over the wire between two provider edges, the receiving edge cannot tell which customer site sent it. Without that, it cannot drop the frames that a leaf should not be sending.

sections.title: The Requirements
sections.content:
Three functional requirements state what a solution must do. It MUST prohibit communication between any two Leaf attachment circuits in an L2VPN instance. It MUST allow multiple Root attachment circuits in an L2VPN instance. And it MUST allow a Root attachment circuit and a Leaf attachment circuit of an L2VPN instance to coexist on any provider edge.

Three further requirements constrain how a solution is built. A solution MUST identify the L2VPN technology to which it applies, naming VPLS or E-VPN. A solution SHOULD minimise the impact on VPLS and E-VPN solutions, especially for the E-LAN services already in operation, and SHOULD be backward compatible with them. It SHOULD allow a case where one L2VPN instance is composed of both provider edges that support the solution and provider edges that do not, with the leaf-to-leaf restriction enforced within the scope of the compliant provider edges only. And a solution SHOULD support the Root Operator Virtual Connection end point, the Leaf Operator Virtual Connection end point and the Trunk Operator Virtual Connection end point specified in the MEF external network network interface specification.
sections.plainLanguage: A solution must block leaf-to-leaf traffic, must allow several roots for redundancy, must allow a root and a leaf on the same router, and must fit into the networks providers already run.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document introduces a requirement to prohibit communication between any two Leaf attachment circuits in an L2VPN instance. In some use cases that requirement is imposed for security reasons. Other than that, there are no additional security considerations beyond those already described for VPLS and E-VPN.
sections.plainLanguage: Blocking leaf-to-leaf traffic is often the security point of the whole exercise. Beyond that, the rules of the existing L2VPN services apply unchanged.
